item.title: Quantum Key Distribution with Entanglement-Swapped Photons from a Quantum Emitter
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Secret key distribution implemented using entanglement-swapped photons from a GaAs quantum dot, yielding an estimated secure key rate of 1×10−3 bit at optimal 30 ps BSM temporal post-selection.

Grade 0.482 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Michele B. Rota, Francesco Basso Basset, Alessandro Laneve, Francesco Salusti, Nicolas Claro-Rodriguez, Giuseppe Ronco, Mattia Beccaceci, Tobias M. Krieger, Quirin Buchinger, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, Sandra Stroj, Mariia Gumberidze, Vladyslav Usenko, Sven Höfling, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Mario A. Usuga Castaneda, Armando Rastelli, Klaus D. Jöns, Rinaldo Trotta

Figure

Quantum bit error rate (QBER) and Bell parameter S plotted against BSM coincidence time window. Shows the trade-off where narrower time windows reduce error and push S above the classical limit of 2.

Asks

Can correlated photons generated from a deterministic quantum emitter and distributed via all-photonic entanglement swapping support secure quantum key distribution?

But

Asymptotic limit. Employs single-emitter temporal multiplexing rather than independent remote quantum dots; requires high temporal filtering (30 ps) to overcome distinguishability limits.

Tools

strain-tuned GaAs/AlGaAs quantum dot in circular Bragg resonator · resonant two-photon excitation (biexciton-exciton cascade) · linear optics Bell state measurement (BSM) · asymmetric source-independent Ekert QKD protocol · high-resolution temporal post-selection

Abstract

Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a fundamental functionality of quantum networks. Extending its range requires quantum repeaters, a technology still under development and not yet demonstrated in combination with quantum cryptographic protocols. Here, we address the elementary operation of a viable quantum repeater scheme by evaluating whether correlated photons distributed via entanglement swapping can support secret key distribution. We employ a state-of-the-art deterministic photon source based on a strain-tuned GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity and implement a source-independent QKD protocol between two nodes using entanglement-swapped photons. We benchmark the system and present how high-resolution temporal post-selection can enable secure key exchange, with further rate improvements expected through realistic device and protocol optimizations. Due to its compatibility with a wide range of quantum memory platforms, our approach represents a significant step towards long-distance quantum-safe communication.

item.title: The QICK Box: A Modular RF Front-End System for Quantum Control and Readout
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Modular companion front-end for AMD ZCU216 RFSoC provides up to 16 outputs, 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases, achieving (91.7±0.4)% single-shot readout fidelity and SNR of 4.4±0.1 without a quantum amplifier.

Grade 0.446 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · L. Arnaldi, D. Martin, S. Sussman, S. Uemura, K. Treptow, N. Wilcer, A. Colón Cesaní, O. Seidel, K. Anyang, G. Bratrud, F. Abouzahr, J. Christiansen-Salameh, D. Baxter, G. Cancelo

Figure

Rotated I-Q scatter plot and projected histograms for 3000 single shots per state (|g⟩ and |e⟩), showing distinct clusters separated by Δμ=28±0.2 a.u. with clean-side noise width σ‾=6.5±0.1 a.u.

Asks

Can an integrated, modular RF/DC companion board for the ZCU216 eliminate external room-temperature signal conditioning while maintaining high-fidelity qubit readout?

But

Readout fidelity limited by T1=58.3±4.1μs relaxation during the 5.6μs readout pulse (causing (4.7±0.3)% error); residual ≈3.6% error from 44 mK effective qubit thermal population and state overlap.

Tools

AMD ZCU216 Gen3 RFSoC FPGA · Modular RF and DC input/output daughtercards · ADMV8818 programmable bandpass filters · PE43705 digital step attenuators · Six-transmon superconducting device

Abstract

The QICK (Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit), first introduced in 2022, is a standalone open source control system for quantum information science. Since then, QICK has been migrated to new hardware platforms, expanded its functionality for applications with different types of qubits (superconducting, atomic, ion-trapped, and spin defects), as well as quantum sensors, and quantum networks. QICK is a highly optimized control kit, with a library of functions that can be used for more than one application. In particular, the software and firmware are customized to minimize latency and maximize control performance and throughput. In this white paper, we describe hardware details and performance of the QICK Box. The QICK Box features up to 16 outputs, up to 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases. Modular output and input daughtercards give the choice of signal chains optimized for fast DC-coupled signals or RF signals up to 10 GHz. Power levels, step attenuation, and bandpass filtering are controlled by software. We demonstrate the system's performance through single-shot readout measurements of a six-transmon device at the Quantum Underground Instrumentation Experimental Testbed (QUIET) at Fermilab, achieving (91.7 +/- 0.4)% readout fidelity limited by T1 decay during the readout. The single shot readout signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is 4.4 +/- 0.1 without a quantum amplifier, confirming that the QICK Box is suitable for high-fidelity quantum control and measurement applications. Advances in firmware and software will be described in a separate paper.

item.title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in S−𝓈 molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.

Grade 0.437 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity” · Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny, Alessandro Chiesa, Stefano Carretta1

Figure

Entanglement infidelity Perr of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time T2 for embedded S=3/2 and S=7/2 units at different relaxation times T1, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.

Asks

How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?

But

Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at Bz=0.35 T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.

Tools

Redfield master equation · Knill–Laflamme conditions · Pauli twirling approximation · Steane [[7,1,3]] code · Star-shaped multi-spin clusters

Abstract

We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

item.title: Extracting the anyon charge from shot noise in complex fractional quantum Hall edges
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Heating corrections to the QPC Fano factor scale as O(𝒯−1/2) for auto-correlation and O(𝒯1/2) for cross-correlation, while a combined clean Fano factor Fclean eliminates outer-arm heating to achieve O(𝒯3/2) scaling and extract the anyon charge e∗/e=1/3.

Grade 0.437 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Jinhong Park, Christian Spranslätt

Figure

Excess current noises ΔSauto, −ΔScross, and resulting Fano factors plotted against dimensionless bias e∗V0/(kBT0). Shows Fclean staying close to e∗/e=1/3 while Fauto diverges and Fcross underestimates the charge.

Asks

How can the intrinsic quasiparticle charge be extracted from shot noise in multichannel fractional quantum Hall edges where intermode equilibration and heating obscure quantum point contact partition noise?

But

Analyzed for the ν=2/3 fractional quantum Hall state in the strong charge-equilibration regime (ℓch≪L) and weak-transmission limit (𝒯≪1).

Tools

discrete network line-junction model · continuum charge and thermal transport equations · four-terminal QPC scattering framework

Abstract

Shot-noise measurements with a quantum point contact provide a direct probe of the quasiparticle charge in Laughlin fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states. However, the interpretation of such measurements becomes more subtle for multichannel edges, where the point-contact tunneling noise coexists with noise generated by intermode equilibration and heating. We develop a general framework that incorporates both these contributions and apply it to the paradigmatic ν=2/3 FQH edge. We derive expressions for the drain auto- and cross-correlations in a four-terminal QPC geometry and show that equilibration-induced heating affects the auto- and cross-correlations in parametrically different way than the intrinsic partition noise. This distinction permits us to propose a specific combination of the two correlations which strongly suppresses the heating contribution and fully recovers the tunneling quasiparticle charge. Our results thereby provide a systematic framework for interpreting shot-noise measurements in complex FQH edges and can be further extended to more general counterpropagating edge structures.

item.title: Design Automation for Gray-Code Quantum Read-Only Memory
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Gray code quantum read-only memory (GQROM) and an automated EDA design flow enable programmable classical data loading into quantum circuits with reduced state-transition complexity.

Grade 0.418 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Hao-Yu Lu, Yu-Ting Kao, Yeong-Jar Chang, Chao-Hung Wang, Darsen D. Lu

Asks

Can Gray-code addressing reduce gate complexity and initialization overhead in quantum read-only memory architectures?

But

Validated via Qiskit simulation.

Tools

Gray code encoding · Qiskit platform · quantum EDA design flow

Abstract

We propose a programmable quantum read-only memory based on Gray code encoding, termed GQROM, designed to efficiently load classical data into quantum circuits. This architecture mitigates critical bottlenecks in near-term quantum computing by reducing initialization overhead and gate-induced errors. By utilizing Gray code, in which consecutive addresses differ by only a single bit, GQROM minimizes state transition complexity. We demonstrate the architecture's flexibility in accessing targeted data through initial-state modification. The entire design, including a systematic EDA flow, was implemented and validated on the Qiskit platform, confirming its practical feasibility. These results underscore GQROM's potential as a scalable and hardware-friendly solution for efficient state preparation in quantum circuits.

item.title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Adding local 𝔰𝔲(D) exchange interactions restores Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing ξ2∝1/N in multi-level spin arrays across spatial dimensions d=1,2,3 for any power-law interaction exponent α.

Grade 0.416 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Sakshi Bahamnia, Sagar Chaudhary, Arman Duha, Thomas Bilitewski

Figure

Minimal spin squeezing parameter ξmin⁡2 and scaling exponent ν versus gap protection strength χ, showing the transition to Heisenberg scaling ξmin⁡2∝1/N in 1D, 2D, and 3D arrays.

Asks

Can gap protection enable Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing in multi-level qudit arrays with finite-range interactions?

Before

Without protection, squeezing scales as ξmin⁡2∝N−ν with ν≈1 only for α≲d/2, degrading to ν≈1/2 at α=d and ν≲0.05 for α≳3d/2.

But

Valid during early-time exponential growth regime before depletion (ni,±1≪1). Assumes periodic boundary conditions and gap-protection strength above critical threshold χ≳χc(L).

Tools

Bogoliubov spin-wave theory · Discrete truncated Wigner approximation (dTWA) · SU(3) Casimir gap protection · Schwinger boson mapping

Abstract

We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local su(D) exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling ξ²∝1/N in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.

item.title: Chiral Vacuum Engineering of Quantum Hall Matter
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Coupling a 2DEG to a chiral cavity isolates resonant from antiresonant vacuum interactions, yielding a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity ρxy(s)=h/(νe2)−sm∗γ2D/(n2De2ωcav2) and an unsqueezed or two-mode squeezed ground state for co- or counter-rotating modes.

Grade 0.404 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…” · Kiran M. Kulkarni, Andrey Baydin, Motoaki Bamba, Junichiro Kono, Ceren B. Dag, Vasil Rokaj

Figure

Polariton eigenspectra, longitudinal resistivity, and Hall resistivity versus magnetic field B for counter-rotating (CRI) and co-rotating (CRA) chiral cavity modes, showing mode crossing versus anticrossing and handedness-dependent Hall corrections.

Asks

How does a circularly polarized, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking chiral cavity vacuum modify the polariton spectrum, ground state, and DC magnetotransport of a two-dimensional electron gas?

Before

In achiral or linearly polarized cavities, Hall resistivity is immune to polariton broadening and light-matter coupling at zero temperature, satisfying ρxyach=h/(νe2).

But

Spatially uniform cavity field (Kohn's theorem center-of-mass coupling), leading order in polariton broadening γ, zero temperature.

Tools

Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian · Hopfield-Bogoliubov diagonalization · SU(2) and SU(1,1) algebraic symmetries · Drude-type DC transport inversion

Abstract

We reveal that a chiral cavity distinguishes the resonant and antiresonant interactions between a two-dimensional electron gas and the cavity vacuum. For co-rotating helicities, the modes anticross, exhibiting vacuum Rabi splitting, and retain a bare vacuum ground state. For counter-rotating helicities, the modes cross, acquiring vacuum-mediated energy shifts and a two-mode squeezed ground state. We trace the origin of these observations to the SU(2) and SU(1,1) symmetries of the respective Hamiltonians and present their spectroscopic signatures in chiral photonic crystal cavities. We further predict that cavity chirality produces a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity at finite polariton broadening, while such a correction is not present in an achiral cavity. For the longitudinal resistivity, we find an asymmetric response of the Shubnikov--de Haas oscillations for the different helicities. Finally, we present an experimentally accessible route for detecting the squeezed ground state through current fluctuations. Parameters based on a recently demonstrated terahertz chiral cavity place these effects within experimental reach.

item.title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Compiling multi-excitonic Bethe-Salpeter equation Hamiltonians into first-quantized block encodings requires O~(N) Toffolis and O(log⁡N) logical qubits, or O~(N) Toffolis and O~(N) qubits. Triexciton eigenvalue estimation in ∼103-atom semiconductors reduces Toffoli counts by 106–107 relative to full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation.

Grade 0.400 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

Figure

Toffoli and logical qubit counts vs k-point mesh size Nk for diamond triexciton (m=3) eigenvalue estimation at 0.1 eV precision, comparing full-Hamiltonian simulation methods with BSE implementations.

Asks

Can quantum simulation of material excited states be made computationally practical on fault-tolerant hardware by operating within a classical quasiparticle Bethe-Salpeter equation framework rather than simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian?

Before

Full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation of a 10×10×10 diamond mesh required 3.7×1017 Toffolis in second quantization (THC) and 4.2×1018 Toffolis in first quantization (plane waves).

But

Heuristic GW/Bethe-Salpeter equation framework with static screened interaction and Tamm-Dancoff approximation; fixed quasiparticle count mtot=2m.

Tools

First-quantized orbital-based block encoding · Tensor hypercontraction (THC) integral factorization · Qubitization · Space-group symmetry adaptation

Abstract

The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size N, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require widetildeO(N) Toffoli gates and O(logN) logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, widetildeO(√N) Toffoli gates and widetildeO(√N) logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of O(10³) atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by 10⁶-10⁷ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.
